detail.extracted_title: From the First Moment: How Omani Hospitals Are Making Parents Full Partners in Neonatal Care
detail.excerpt: Backed by four years of clinical outcomes at Khoula Hospital and international patient-experience recognition, Omani neonatologists are placing mothers and fathers at the center of intensive care for premature newborns.
detail.article_html:
For parents of a premature newborn, walking into a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) for the first time can feel like crossing into an unfamiliar world of monitors, incubators, and clinical terminology. For decades, conventional intensive care protocols treated mothers and fathers primarily as visitors during restricted hours. Today, neonatal specialists across the Sultanate of Oman are reshaping that model from the ground up, bringing parents directly into the daily medical and developmental care plan of their infants.

Convened in Muscat under the theme "From the First Moment, the Care Experience Begins" and patronized by Dr. Yousuf bin Salim Al-Hinai, Head of the Performance and Government Follow-up Unit at the General Secretariat of the Council of Ministers, the Conference on Developing the Family Experience in Neonatal Care brought together neonatologists, pediatric neurologists, nurses, and patient-experience leaders from Oman and Saudi Arabia. The two-day gathering examined how responsive, family-centered care improves survival, neurological development, and emotional resilience for premature infants and their families.

Parents as Indispensable Partners in the NICU

Opening the conference, Dr. Abeer bint Abdullah Al-Maamari, Head of the National Patient Experience Project Team at the Ministry of Health, emphasized that inside neonatal intensive care units, parents are essential partners in their child's therapeutic journey. Moving from institution-centered care to responsive, person-centered care requires listening closely to families' cultural and emotional needs and involving them in clinical decision-making from day one.

That national shift toward humanizing hospital care recently earned international recognition: the Ministry of Health received an Honorable Mention in the Leadership and Management Award from the International Hospital Federation for 2026 for its project developing the patient experience in Omani hospitals, in alignment with the health governance goals of Oman Vision 2040.

Clinical Evidence: Weight Gain, Breastfeeding, and Early Discharge

The push to integrate parents into NICU routines rests on measurable clinical outcomes. Dr. Mohammed Abdul Latif, Senior Consultant Neonatologist at Sultan Qaboos University, presented evidence showing that structured family-integrated care—where nurses and physicians coach parents to participate in daily care inside the unit—leads directly to improved infant weight gain, higher rates of exclusive breastfeeding, lower maternal and paternal stress, and greater readiness for a safe transition home.

Midwife specialist Fahima Al-Harthi highlighted the vital role of nursing and midwifery teams in providing continuous emotional support, clear medical communication, and early skin-to-skin contact for mothers navigating premature birth. To measure how effectively intensive care units meet these standards, Dr. Salim Al-Shukaili outlined the cultural adaptation of international neonatal family-satisfaction instruments, including the EMPATHIC-N scale, alongside Empathy-Based Practice (EBP) frameworks tailored to Omani family life.

Four Years of Khoula Hospital's Developmental Follow-Up Clinic

Care for a premature infant does not end at hospital discharge. Dr. Marwa Al-Balushi reviewed the four-year track record of the Developmental Follow-Up Clinic for Children at Khoula Hospital, established in 2022 as a dedicated multidisciplinary model for premature and high-risk newborns.

Rather than waiting for developmental delays to appear later in childhood, the Khoula Hospital clinic evaluates infants early and repeatedly using internationally validated neurological and developmental assessments, including the Prechtl General Movements Assessment (GMA), the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination (HINE), and the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (Bayley-4). When subtle motor or cognitive challenges are detected, infants begin targeted physical and occupational therapy immediately, with parents trained as primary co-therapists at home. By uniting advanced neonatal medicine with the irreplaceable presence of a mother and father, Omani hospitals are ensuring that the smallest patients begin life surrounded by both clinical excellence and family warmth.

detail.instagram_caption:
When a newborn arrives prematurely, the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) can feel overwhelming for mothers and fathers. In Muscat, healthcare leaders, neonatologists, and midwifery specialists have gathered under the theme "From the First Moment, the Care Experience Begins" to advance a model where parents are active partners in their infant's daily medical and developmental treatment plan.

Clinical studies presented by specialists from Sultan Qaboos University and the Ministry of Health demonstrate that involving parents directly inside the NICU improves infant weight gain, strengthens breastfeeding, lowers parental anxiety, and prepares families for a safer transition home. Meanwhile, Khoula Hospital's Developmental Follow-Up Clinic, established in 2022, uses international neurological scales (GMA, HINE, and Bayley-4) to provide early intervention and empower Omani parents as co-therapists throughout early childhood.

How can hospitals continue to make intensive care units more welcoming and supportive for families?

Read the full analysis at omanspire.om (link in bio).
